audit: The service-counter analogy suggests that a correct form and a receipt are helpful, but readers need to see the checks and the limits of that receipt. Lesson A uses exact INR minor units, an authenticated principal and a pending approval to show a valid request that must wait. Lesson B holds a lost refund response constant while varying the downstream effect contract. An atomic deduplication service can return the original result; a service without safe status or retry semantics leaves the effect unknown. This preserves the distinction between local identity, external execution guarantees and ordinary narrative evidence.

lessons.title: The counter accepts a form, not permission
lessons.intro: Customer C-7 owns ORD-104233. A refund request passes local validation and current eligibility, but its exact financial effect still needs review.

checks.label: Arguments + evidence
checks.detail: Strict schema and retained evidence IDs valid

checks.label: Exact approval
checks.detail: P-6 has no authenticated review decision

data.result: Persist proposal P-6; release worker; no refund yet

read: The principal comes from authenticated runtime context, not generated fields.
Exact amount and currency define the financial proposal.
Passing eligibility does not satisfy the missing approval.
lessons.question: If the model adds approved=true to its arguments, can the counter issue the refund?
lessons.answer: No. The strict request contract rejects unrecognized fields, and approval must come through an authenticated review path bound to P-6. Even a structurally accepted request cannot grant its own execution authority.
lessons.takeaway: Tool contracts express intended work; trusted checks decide whether it may execute.
lessons.assumption: Fictional INR example with 100 minor units per rupee. Evidence IDs are retained separately; the four displayed fields are a projection.

lessons.title: A receipt key needs a downstream contract
lessons.intro: The payment request using accepted intent K-17 timed out. The runtime cannot tell whether the provider committed its refund.

data.input: K-17 submitted; response lost; local result is unknown

left.title: Atomic key support
steps: Retain the exact intent and original K-17
left.result: Record confirmed RF-9; one intended refund effect

right.title: No safe retry contract
steps: Status lookup cannot resolve the submission
right.result: Outcome remains unknown; no blind resubmission

read: Both paths begin with the same saved intent and lost response.
The left result depends on provider enforcement and retained key semantics.
The right path preserves uncertainty instead of inventing success or absence.
lessons.question: If the model rewrites only its explanation, should recovery create a new key?
lessons.answer: No. The accepted effect is unchanged. Reuse its retained identity under the applicable provider contract. A changed narrative must not turn recovery into a new financial operation, and a local hash alone supplies no external deduplication guarantee.
lessons.takeaway: Unknown outcomes require effect-aware recovery, not a new proposal with new wording.
lessons.assumption: Fictional alternatives; the left service guarantees atomic key matching within retention. The right service offers no conclusive status or safe retry.
